title: FIFO
body:
The word does two jobs in this course. Both are real, they are related, and mixing them up
is easy.

## 1. The queue discipline (what this course usually means)

First in, first out: the element that has been waiting longest is the one that leaves next.
It is the ordering rule of a [[Queue]], as opposed to a [[Stack]]'s last in, first out.

Where it shows up here:

- A [[Wait Queue]] is FIFO. Waking the longest-waiting process is what gives
  [[Bounded Waiting]] its bound and therefore what prevents [[Starvation]].
- A [[Ready Queue]] at one [[Process Priority]] level is FIFO, and running its front
  process for one time slice before requeueing it at the back is round robin.
- FCFS scheduling is FIFO applied to the whole ready queue with no preemption, see
  [[CPU Scheduling]].

FIFO is the *fair* discipline, which is exactly why the kernel uses it wherever fairness is
a correctness requirement rather than a preference.

## 2. The named pipe

A FIFO is also the Unix name for a **named pipe**: a pipe that exists as an entry in the
[[File Systems|file system]], so unrelated processes can open it by path instead of having
to be parent and child. `mkfifo /tmp/mypipe`, then one process writes to it and another
reads. The data still never touches the disk.

That sense belongs to [[Piping]], which owns the pipe material; it is called a FIFO because
bytes come out in the order they went in, so it is really sense 1 applied to a stream.
